answer.rationale: The strongest signal here is temporal: a release landed 2 hours ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago, which is consistent with the release being causal (deploy, then ramp as settlement traffic loaded the new build). Among the five candidate directions, rollback is the only one that addresses a suspected code-introduced regression rather than a capacity or dependency failure. Regional failover (memory_b2) treats a region-localized degradation, but a bad build is present in every region, so failover would carry the defect with the traffic and risk write loss during a peak settlement window. Capacity headroom (memory_b3) helped a demand surge with flat queue depth; nothing here indicates a demand-side surge rather than a per-write cost increase. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) helped when an external partner dependency was failing; no partner failure is reported, and failing fast on the write path during settlement peak directly threatens the objective of not losing customer writes. Read-replica routing (memory_b5) relieves read pressure on the primary, but the reported symptom is write-path latency and writes are heavy, so it is at best partial and at worst irrelevant. I am spending my one verification on memory_b1 because it is the memory my chosen action leans on most heavily, and its summary carries the most decision-relevant compression risk: 'the prior build was stable and the rollback finished without customer impact' may be hiding preconditions I cannot see. Specifically I want the original record to tell me whether that day-18 rollback happened during a low-traffic period rather than a settlement peak, whether the release involved schema or data-format migrations (a forward-only migration would make rollback unsafe or write-destructive), and whether 'without customer impact' meant zero dropped writes or merely no error-rate spike. If the archive shows day 18 was a quiet-window rollback of a migration-free build, my confidence rises materially; if it involved a migration or was rolled back off-peak, rollback may be the wrong move at peak and I would fall back to the least-destructive partial mitigation. I did not verify memory_b6 despite using it, because staged-gating precedent supports the shape of my action rather than its safety, and it is the safety precondition that could invalidate the plan. Downstream value risk: two concerns. First, an inherited-memory anchoring risk — every memory in this store is a success story, so I am reasoning from a survivorship-biased record with no failed-rollback or failed-failover cases to calibrate against, which likely inflates my prior on all five actions. Second, an operational risk: a rollback during peak settlement can abandon in-flight writes or, if the release included a forward migration, corrupt or orphan records written under the new schema, which would violate the do-not-lose-customer-writes constraint more severely than elevated latency does. For that reason I am scoping this as a small guarded test rather than a fleet-wide revert: roll back one canary cell or a single shard first, with write draining and reconciliation checks, and confirm p99 recovery on that slice before committing further. Uncertainty preserved: I have not established causation, only correlation in timing. The alternative hypothesis is that settlement peak alone is saturating the write path and the release is coincidental, in which case rollback yields nothing and I have burned my single intervention. The guarded scope is chosen precisely so that a null result is cheap and informative rather than costly, and I am explicitly recording that a migration finding in the day-18 record should override this plan.
